cards.prompt: Limbic system & basal ganglia
cards.promptHtml: Limbic system & basal ganglia
cards.answerHtml:
Limbic system:

  • Hippocampus: stores emotional aspects of memory
  • Thalamus: relays/filters all sensory input except smell
  • Hypothalamus: regulates sleep, temperature, hunger, thirst, sex drive; works with pituitary to control endocrine function
  • Amygdala: adds emotion to memory; modulates aggression and sexuality

Basal ganglia / extrapyramidal system: control motor tone, reflexes, automatic movement (putamen, globus pallidus, caudate); psychotropic drugs can affect this system, the anatomic basis of drug-induced movement side effects

cards.prompt: Dopamine pathways
cards.promptHtml: Dopamine pathways
cards.answerHtml:
Blocking dopamine in:

  • Mesolimbic: reduces overactivity linked to psychosis (treatment target)
  • Nigrostriatal: disrupts extrapyramidal motor control, causing movement side effects
  • Tuberoinfundibular: raises prolactin, causing galactorrhea, amenorrhea, sexual dysfunction

cards.prompt: Receptor actions & downregulation
cards.promptHtml: Receptor actions & downregulation
cards.answerHtml:
Agonist: mimics the natural chemical, same response (selectivity, affinity, intrinsic activity)

Antagonist: blocks the receptor's response (selectivity and affinity only, no intrinsic activity)

Partial agonist: binds with weak intrinsic activity, smaller response than a full agonist

Downregulation: receptor subsensitivity from decreased response to continued stimulation; helps explain why benefits take weeks and effects can diminish

cards.prompt: Pharmacokinetics: steady state & CYP450
cards.promptHtml: Pharmacokinetics: steady state & CYP450
cards.answerHtml:
Steady state: drug intake equals elimination, so plasma level stops rising; takes about 4-5 half-lives. More than 90% clears in at least 4 half-lives after stopping.

CYP450 inhibitor: slows metabolism of another drug, raising its level

CYP450 inducer: speeds metabolism of another drug, lowering its level

  • Example: cigarette smoke induces CYP1A2, lowering some drug levels (e.g., clozapine); a patient who quits smoking can see those levels and side effects rise

cards.prompt: Pharmacogenomics & ethnopsychopharmacology
cards.promptHtml: Pharmacogenomics & ethnopsychopharmacology
cards.answerHtml:
Pharmacogenomics: how genetic makeup affects drug response

  • Poor metabolizers: break drug down slowly; risk toxicity at standard doses
  • Rapid metabolizers: clear it quickly; may never reach a therapeutic level

Ethnopsychopharmacology: how culture and genetic differences among groups influence response

  • Example: some people of Asian descent need one-half to one-third the typical antipsychotic dose, and lower antidepressant doses

cards.prompt: Neurotransmitters & clinical associations
cards.promptHtml: Neurotransmitters & clinical associations
cards.answerHtml:
• Loss of acetylcholine: Alzheimer disease
  • Low serotonin: depression
  • Low GABA: anxiety/seizures
  • High dopamine: psychosis
  • Low dopamine: Parkinson disease

Excitatory vs inhibitory: Boyd calls dopamine excitatory and serotonin primarily excitatory (Psych Notes: both inhibitory). GABA (inhibitory) and glutamate (excitatory) are the safe fixed pair to memorize.

cards.prompt: Psychopharmacology basics
cards.promptHtml: Psychopharmacology basics
cards.answerHtml:
Target symptom: specific, measurable symptom expected to improve (not the diagnosis); document before and during treatment

Same drug class, many diagnoses: symptoms (e.g., agitation) cross diagnoses

Augmentation: adding a drug for partial response

FDA phases:

  • I: dose tolerance in healthy volunteers
  • II: effective dose range in limited group with the disorder
  • III: large multisite efficacy trials
  • IV: post-marketing surveillance (rare reactions)

cards.prompt: Phases of psychotropic treatment
cards.promptHtml: Phases of psychotropic treatment
cards.answerHtml:
• Initiation: psychiatric evaluation, cultural assessment, baseline labs; first dose is a 'test dose'
  • Stabilization: titration, monitor target symptoms/side effects, therapeutic drug monitoring
  • Maintenance: relapse prevention, patient self-monitoring
  • Discontinuation: may require tapering

Test dose: monitor vital signs, mental status, allergic reaction, ataxia

cards.prompt: Patient wants to stop or refuses medication
cards.promptHtml: Patient wants to stop or refuses medication
cards.answerHtml:
Wants to stop (side effect): assess the side effect and report to prescriber; do not withhold the drug on your own authority or just say 'it will go away' (missed doses risk relapse and discontinuation symptoms)

Who decides: the patient (recovery-oriented care); nurse gives honest, evidence-based information, no coercion

Competent patient refuses: nurse cannot give it anyway, except in emergencies or as permitted by law; links to right to treatment in the least restrictive environment

cards.prompt: Nonadherence: reasons & strategies
cards.promptHtml: Nonadherence: reasons & strategies
cards.answerHtml:
Most-cited reason for stopping: side effects

  • Others: lack of illness awareness, stigma, feeling better, confusion about dosing, access problems, substance use

Strategies:

  • Prompt management of side effects
  • Long-acting injectables and simplified dosing
  • Psychoeducation tied to personal goals (e.g., keeping a job)
  • Solve access barriers (e.g., home lab draws for limited transportation)

Psychoeducation groups: nurse-led medication teaching in a group; most effective when tied to the person's symptoms and goals

cards.prompt: Family response & home management
cards.promptHtml: Family response & home management
cards.answerHtml:
Family says 'she's better, she doesn't need it': families may deny illness or mistake symptom control for a cure, especially with visible side effects; nurse includes family in teaching and consent discussions, does not dismiss the comment

Home management plan:

  • Emergency contact numbers, reviewed frequently with patient and family
  • When adherence risk is high: simplified dosing schedules, lab draws closer to home

cards.prompt: Giving oral psychotropics: juice & antacids
cards.promptHtml: Giving oral psychotropics: juice & antacids
cards.answerHtml:
Liquid concentrates: can precipitate in acidic juices, altering the dose delivered; check compatibility before mixing

Antacids: can reduce absorption of antipsychotics; separate dosing: antacid at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after the psychotropic

cards.prompt: Nutrition effects of psychotropics
cards.promptHtml: Nutrition effects of psychotropics
cards.answerHtml:
Assess for:

  • Weight gain
  • Fluid and electrolyte imbalances
  • Constipation
  • Drug incompatibilities with liquids

Constipation teaching:

  • Increase fiber and fluids
  • Regular exercise
  • Bulk laxative with at least 16 oz of fluid if needed

cards.prompt: Older adults: polypharmacy & advertising
cards.promptHtml: Older adults: polypharmacy & advertising
cards.answerHtml:
Polypharmacy: five or more medications; affects up to 90% of long-term care residents ages 62-85; about one-third of residents in one facility took 8-16 drugs daily

Direct-to-consumer advertising (verify): can raise unrealistic expectations or requests for a specific advertised drug; nurse gives balanced, evidence-based information rather than reinforcing marketing claims
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Older adults: start low, go slow
cards.promptHtml: Older adults: start low, go slow
cards.answerHtml:
Why lower doses and slower titration:

  • Body fat up and total body water down: fat-soluble drugs accumulate
  • Renal and hepatic function decline: slower clearance
  • Albumin drops: more free/active drug
  • Anticholinergic sensitivity rises

cards.prompt: Trends in psychopharmacology
cards.promptHtml: Trends in psychopharmacology
cards.answerHtml:
• Long-acting injectables: one injection every 2 weeks to 3 months; steady blood level between doses, nothing daily to remember
  • Digital adherence: aripiprazole tablet with an ingestible sensor, wearable sensor and app that confirm doses taken (still being studied)
  • Telehealth and mobile apps: remote counseling, medication and side-effect reviews; effectiveness still being evaluated

cards.prompt: Psychotic-disorder duration ladder: brief psychotic disorder vs. schizophreniform disorder vs. schizophrenia?
cards.promptHtml: Psychotic-disorder duration ladder: brief psychotic disorder vs. schizophreniform disorder vs. schizophrenia?
cards.answerHtml:
• Brief psychotic disorder: 1 day to under 1 month; sudden onset, full return to baseline
  • Schizophreniform disorder: 1 month to under 6 months
  • Schizophrenia: 6+ months continuous (incl. 1+ month active symptoms), with marked functional decline

cards.prompt: Brief psychotic disorder
cards.promptHtml: Brief psychotic disorder
cards.answerHtml: Psychotic symptoms lasting at least 1 day but less than 1 month, with sudden onset (may follow a severe stressor) and a full return to baseline functioning. Suicide risk is high, especially in younger patients.

cards.prompt: Schizophreniform disorder
cards.promptHtml: Schizophreniform disorder
cards.answerHtml: Same symptom criteria as schizophrenia (2+ of: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized/catatonic behavior, negative symptoms), but lasts 1 to under 6 months. About 1/3 fully recover; about 2/3 progress to schizophrenia.

cards.prompt: Schizoaffective disorder
cards.promptHtml: Schizoaffective disorder
cards.answerHtml: A major mood episode (depressive or manic) occurs together with psychosis, PLUS at least 2 weeks of delusions/hallucinations occur without a major mood episode present; mood symptoms are present most of the time. It carries a better long-term outcome and social functioning than schizophrenia.

cards.prompt: Substance/medication-induced psychotic disorder
cards.promptHtml: Substance/medication-induced psychotic disorder
cards.answerHtml: Psychosis due to substance intoxication or withdrawal, but more severe than typically expected for that intoxication/withdrawal. Hallucinations/delusions persist as long as the substance is used (withdrawal effects can last weeks), so a differential diagnosis is recommended.

cards.prompt: Schizophreniform disorder vs. brief psychotic disorder: what differentiates these?
cards.promptHtml: Schizophreniform disorder vs. brief psychotic disorder: what differentiates these?
cards.answerHtml: Duration and course. Brief psychotic disorder lasts at least 1 day but less than 1 month, with sudden onset and full return to baseline. Schizophreniform disorder lasts 1 to under 6 months with schizophrenia-level symptoms and an uncertain outcome.

cards.prompt: Schizophrenia vs. schizophreniform disorder: what differentiates these?
cards.promptHtml: Schizophrenia vs. schizophreniform disorder: what differentiates these?
cards.answerHtml: Duration only — both share the same symptom criteria. Schizophrenia requires continuous disturbance for 6+ months (with 1+ month active). Schizophreniform disorder lasts 1 month to under 6 months; about 1/3 recover and 2/3 progress to schizophrenia.

cards.prompt: Schizoaffective disorder vs. schizophrenia: what differentiates these?
cards.promptHtml: Schizoaffective disorder vs. schizophrenia: what differentiates these?
cards.answerHtml: Schizoaffective disorder requires a major mood episode (depressive or manic) occurring together with psychosis, PLUS at least 2 weeks of psychosis without the mood episode present. Schizophrenia is diagnosed only after schizoaffective and mood disorders with psychotic features are ruled out; it requires 6+ months of continuous signs.

cards.prompt: Schizoaffective disorder vs. a mood disorder with psychotic features: what differentiates these?
cards.promptHtml: Schizoaffective disorder vs. a mood disorder with psychotic features: what differentiates these?
cards.answerHtml: In schizoaffective disorder, psychosis (delusions/hallucinations) occurs for at least 2 weeks WITHOUT a major mood episode, yet mood symptoms are present most of the time; these patients are more likely to have persistent psychosis than those with a mood disorder. In a mood disorder with psychotic features, the psychosis is tied to and occurs only alongside the mood episode (verify).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Substance/medication-induced psychotic disorder vs. schizophrenia: what differentiates these?
cards.promptHtml: Substance/medication-induced psychotic disorder vs. schizophrenia: what differentiates these?
cards.answerHtml: Substance/medication-induced psychotic disorder: psychosis due to intoxication or withdrawal, more severe than expected, persisting as long as the substance is used (withdrawal effects can last weeks). Schizophrenia is diagnosed only after substances and medical conditions are ruled out, with 6+ months of continuous signs.

cards.prompt: Delusional disorder vs. schizophrenia: what differentiates these?
cards.promptHtml: Delusional disorder vs. schizophrenia: what differentiates these?
cards.answerHtml: Delusional disorder requires 1+ month of well-systematized delusions, behavior not bizarre; functioning stays intact apart from the delusion's direct effects (patients often live with it for years, rarely seeking treatment). Schizophrenia requires 2+ core symptom domains and causes broad functional decline.

cards.prompt: What are the five DSM-IV subtypes of schizophrenia?
cards.promptHtml: What are the five DSM-IV subtypes of schizophrenia?
cards.answerHtml:
Lecture: DSM-5-TR has no subtypes; syllabus and Psych Notes still list these (descriptions: verify).

  • Paranoid: persecutory/grandiose delusions, frequent auditory hallucinations; later onset, better prognosis
  • Disorganized: disorganized speech/behavior, flat or inappropriate affect; early onset, poor prognosis
  • Catatonic: stupor, mutism, waxy flexibility, posturing; physiologic needs first
  • Undifferentiated: active symptoms present but don't fit the other patterns
  • Residual: past episode; negative symptoms persist, no prominent positive symptoms
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Delusional disorder subtypes
cards.promptHtml: Delusional disorder subtypes
cards.answerHtml:
Core: 1+ month of non-bizarre, well-systematized delusions; functioning intact apart from the delusion

Subtypes (by main theme):

  • Erotomanic: a higher-status person is in love with them
  • Grandiose: inflated worth, power, knowledge or special identity
  • Jealous: sexual partner is unfaithful
  • Persecutory: being malevolently treated
  • Somatic: has a physical defect or disease
  • Mixed: no single predominant theme

cards.prompt: How does schizophrenia progress from the prodromal period into the acute phase?
cards.promptHtml: How does schizophrenia progress from the prodromal period into the acute phase?
cards.answerHtml:
• Prodromal: tension/nervousness, poor appetite, trouble concentrating, disturbed sleep, decreased enjoyment, restlessness, forgetfulness, depression, social withdrawal, feeling laughed at; negative symptoms appear before positive ones but are harder to date
  • Acute: subtle behavior turns bizarre/disruptive — not sleeping for days, incoherent speech, aggression, frightening delusions/hallucinations; self-care breaks down. Nursing priority: safety (suicide/aggression risk) plus starting medication

cards.prompt: List the three phases of schizophrenia and the main focus of care in each.
cards.promptHtml: List the three phases of schizophrenia and the main focus of care in each.
cards.answerHtml:
• Acute: safety and symptom control (high suicide/aggression risk); medication started promptly, low-stimulus environment
  • Stabilization: establishing the medication regimen (6-12 week trial), eliminating substance use, side-effect management
  • Maintenance/recovery: relapse prevention, psychosocial functioning, quality of life, hope

cards.prompt: What are positive, negative, and cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia, with one example of each?
cards.promptHtml: What are positive, negative, and cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia, with one example of each?
cards.answerHtml:
• Positive: excess/distortion of normal function — e.g., hallucinations, delusions
  • Negative: loss of normal function — e.g., flat affect, avolition, alogia, anhedonia
  • Cognitive: impaired memory, attention, and executive function; can occur independent of positive/negative symptoms and predicts poor functional outcome

cards.prompt: Schizophrenia suicide risk
cards.promptHtml: Schizophrenia suicide risk
cards.answerHtml:
• About 50% attempt suicide
  • 10-15% die by suicide (Psych Notes: 9-13%)
  • About 4.5 times the general-population risk
  • Highest in the acute phase; hospitalization may be needed for safety
  • Life span about 20 years shorter on average (Boyd: up to 20)

cards.prompt: Differentiate these disorganized-speech terms: loose associations, tangentiality, circumstantiality, word salad, neologism, and clang association.
cards.promptHtml: Differentiate these disorganized-speech terms: loose associations, tangentiality, circumstantiality, word salad, neologism, and clang association.
cards.answerHtml:
• Loose associations: sudden topic shifts with no apparent link, patient unaware
  • Tangentiality: a logical-seeming topic change that never gets back to the point
  • Circumstantiality: excessive detail, but the person eventually reaches the point
  • Word salad: words strung together with no connection
  • Neologism: a made-up word with no common meaning
  • Clang association: words chosen only because they rhyme or sound alike (e.g., "right, light, sight, might")

cards.prompt: Differentiate these schizophrenia signs: hallucination vs. delusion, echolalia vs. echopraxia, and catatonia/waxy flexibility.
cards.promptHtml: Differentiate these schizophrenia signs: hallucination vs. delusion, echolalia vs. echopraxia, and catatonia/waxy flexibility.
cards.answerHtml:
• Hallucination: a perceptual experience (often auditory) with no external stimulus; delusion: a fixed, false belief (thoughts only) unchanged by reasonable argument
  • Echolalia: parrot-like repetition of another's words; echopraxia: involuntary imitation of another's movements and gestures (ATI: purposeful)
  • Catatonia: psychomotor disturbance (stupor, mutism, posturing, repetitive behavior); waxy flexibility: a posture held in an odd fixed position for long periods, e.g. where someone else placed a limb

cards.prompt: Differentiate these negative-symptom terms: anhedonia, avolition, alogia, and flat affect.
cards.promptHtml: Differentiate these negative-symptom terms: anhedonia, avolition, alogia, and flat affect.
cards.answerHtml:
• Anhedonia: inability to experience pleasure or joy
  • Avolition: lack of motivation for goal-directed behavior/hygiene — a negative symptom often mistaken for laziness; motivation, not lost skill, is the barrier to hygiene
  • Alogia: reduced fluency/productivity of thought and speech (poverty of speech)
  • Flat affect: emotional expression is absent — facial expression never changes (distinct from "blunted" affect, where expression is present but greatly diminished)

cards.prompt: What happens if a patient with schizophrenia stops medication, and what should a relapse-prevention plan include?
cards.promptHtml: What happens if a patient with schizophrenia stops medication, and what should a relapse-prevention plan include?
cards.answerHtml:
• Relapse is nearly guaranteed once medication stops; each relapse takes longer to recover from than the one before
  • Triggers also include psychosocial stress, poor community resources, stigma, and social isolation
  • A relapse-prevention plan teaches the patient to recognize personal triggers and early symptom changes

cards.prompt: Schizophrenia target symptoms and rating scales
cards.promptHtml: Schizophrenia target symptoms and rating scales
cards.answerHtml:
Target symptoms / associated findings (Boyd):

  • Inappropriate affect, loss of pleasure, dysphoric mood
  • Disturbed sleep; refusing food
  • Poor concentration, confusion, memory impairment
  • Lack of insight; depersonalization, derealization
  • Motor abnormalities

Track response with scales: SAPS (positive), SANS (negative), PANSS, BPRS; AIMS/DISCUS for movement side effects

cards.prompt: Schizophrenia prevalence and age at diagnosis
cards.promptHtml: Schizophrenia prevalence and age at diagnosis
cards.answerHtml:
Global prevalence: 0.2-0.7% (lecture) (Boyd: about 0.48%, range 0.34-0.85%)

Age at diagnosis: men 18-25, women 25-35

Risk: first-degree relatives have 10x the risk

Children: rare; often missed

cards.prompt: Schizophrenia biologic theories: dopamine and hypofrontality
cards.promptHtml: Schizophrenia biologic theories: dopamine and hypofrontality
cards.answerHtml:
Dopamine hypothesis:

  • Too much dopamine (D2) in the mesolimbic tract: positive symptoms
  • Too little dopamine in the prefrontal cortex: cognitive dysfunction

Hypofrontality: reduced blood flow and glucose metabolism in the prefrontal cortex on PET

Other findings (lecture): larger lateral and third ventricles, smaller total brain volume; glutamate/GABA role (PCP mimics psychosis)

cards.prompt: Schizophrenia nursing assessment areas
cards.promptHtml: Schizophrenia nursing assessment areas
cards.answerHtml:
• Physical health: rule out underlying medical causes
  • Nutrition and sleep: disruptions compound each other
  • Trauma history
  • Medications: baseline movement exam before starting (AIMS, DISCUS, Simpson-Angus)
  • Substance use
  • Phase of illness and psychosocial cues
  • Positive and negative symptoms, past and present
  • Strengths: family and social supports

cards.prompt: How should the nurse respond to a patient's hallucinations and delusions?
cards.promptHtml: How should the nurse respond to a patient's hallucinations and delusions?
cards.answerHtml:
• Hallucinations: always ask what the voices are saying first — especially whether they are command hallucinations telling the patient to harm self or others; content/intent must be assessed first for safety
  • Delusions: never argue or try to disprove the belief, and never pretend to share it; acknowledge the feeling behind it ("that sounds frightening") and offer safety/reassurance without agreeing it's true

cards.prompt: What is 'high expressed emotion' in families, and what does family psychoeducation emphasize?
cards.promptHtml: What is 'high expressed emotion' in families, and what does family psychoeducation emphasize?
cards.answerHtml:
• High expressed emotion: a family pattern of criticism, hostility, or overinvolvement toward the patient; patients can relapse even on medication when living with it
  • Medication plus psychosocial treatment greatly reduces how often and how severely relapse occurs; the single most important point taught is consistent medication taking, alongside disease course, treatment, support systems, life-management skills, and expecting relapse

cards.prompt: Why is medication adherence described as critical for people with schizophrenia, apart from preventing relapse?
cards.promptHtml: Why is medication adherence described as critical for people with schizophrenia, apart from preventing relapse?
cards.answerHtml: Medication reduces symptoms and lets the person work toward recovery, but it does not cure the illness. Treatment is usually lifelong, and adherence is the best available way to prevent relapse and the functional decline that comes with it.

cards.prompt: Errorless learning in schizophrenia
cards.promptHtml: Errorless learning in schizophrenia
cards.answerHtml:
What: give the correct information directly, then have the patient write it down; no guessing or trial and error

Why: learning lasts longer when it happens without errors; cognitive deficits make guessing ineffective

How: low-distraction setting, clear words, simple visuals, small segments with frequent reinforcement, only when the patient is ready

cards.prompt: Non-drug treatments for schizophrenia
cards.promptHtml: Non-drug treatments for schizophrenia
cards.answerHtml:
• Cognitive training/remediation: targets cognitive deficits and social functioning
  • Social skills training: lecture, demonstration, role-play, homework; break tasks into small steps; wait for a lucid period if actively psychotic
  • Supported employment: most effective vocational rehabilitation method
  • Milieu therapy
  • Lecture list: counseling for delusions/hallucinations, conflict resolution, behavior therapy, mindfulness/coping

cards.prompt: ECT in schizophrenia
cards.promptHtml: ECT in schizophrenia
cards.answerHtml:
Most useful when the patient is:

  • Catatonic
  • Depressed
  • Medication resistant
  • Assaultive
  • Psychotic

cards.prompt: Building trust with a patient with schizophrenia
cards.promptHtml: Building trust with a patient with schizophrenia
cards.answerHtml:
• Calm, caring approach from the first encounter
  • Short, time-limited interactions during psychosis
  • Be consistent and follow through on every promise
  • A patient who denies being ill may still take medication and attend treatment because they trust the nurse

cards.prompt: Support groups in schizophrenia
cards.promptHtml: Support groups in schizophrenia
cards.answerHtml:
• Focus on daily problems and the stress of living with mental illness
  • Useful across the continuum of care and reduce suicide risk
  • Hospital: simply sharing the experience of the illness
  • Community: regular contact with people facing the same issues; friendships often form
  • Peer support is part of recovery-oriented care

cards.prompt: Three common problems of severe mental illness
cards.promptHtml: Three common problems of severe mental illness
cards.answerHtml:
• Nonadherence and relapse: stopping medication almost always leads to relapse
  • Medical comorbidity: diabetes, metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease; life span about 20 years shorter
  • Poverty, unemployment, housing problems: clustering in lower-income groups; isolation and stigma

(Substance and tobacco use are also common.)

cards.prompt: Evidence-based practices for severe mental illness
cards.promptHtml: Evidence-based practices for severe mental illness
cards.answerHtml:
• Assertive Community Treatment (ACT): 24-hour multidisciplinary team brings services to the patient (home visits, transportation, job support); solid evidence; fewer hospital days
  • Intensive case management: small caseloads
  • Supported employment
  • Self-management: symptom monitoring and relapse prevention
  • Early treatment of first-episode psychosis in a comprehensive program

cards.prompt: Community and home care in schizophrenia
cards.promptHtml: Community and home care in schizophrenia
cards.answerHtml:
Community options: partial hospitalization, day treatment, crisis stabilization, ACT, case management, clubhouses

Continuity: many states require an outpatient appointment before discharge

Home care nurse assesses: mental status, the environment, medication adherence, family dynamics and home safety; draws labs; crisis intervention to prevent readmission

Also: make sure the patient gets primary medical care

cards.prompt: Older adults with schizophrenia
cards.promptHtml: Older adults with schizophrenia
cards.answerHtml:
• Symptoms may improve and relapses lessen with age
  • More likely to develop cognitive impairment
  • Outcome depends on earlier treatment and support systems
  • Community services for older adults have developed more slowly
  • Assess for underlying medical disorders that may relate to the symptoms (lecture)

cards.prompt: Schizophrenia and nutrition
cards.promptHtml: Schizophrenia and nutrition
cards.answerHtml:
Illness effects: food refusal or fear of eating (poisoning delusions); can become undernourished

Suspicious patient:

  • Canned or prepackaged food, own can opener
  • Family-style meals so they see others eat the same food
  • Let them examine food or help prepare it

Also: nutrition and sleep problems compound each other

cards.prompt: What are the DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder (MDD)?
cards.promptHtml: What are the DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder (MDD)?
cards.answerHtml:
• 5+ of 9 symptoms during the same 2-week period
  • At least one must be depressed mood OR anhedonia (loss of interest/pleasure)
  • Change from baseline; causes significant distress/impairment
  • SIGECAPS: Sleep, Interest, Guilt, Energy, Concentration, Appetite, Psychomotor change, Suicidal ideation
  • Must never have had a manic/hypomanic episode

cards.prompt: How do persistent depressive disorder, seasonal affective disorder, and peripartum-onset episodes differ from MDD?
cards.promptHtml: How do persistent depressive disorder, seasonal affective disorder, and peripartum-onset episodes differ from MDD?
cards.answerHtml:
• Dysthymia: chronic, lower-grade symptoms most days ≥2 years (1 yr children); full MDD episode on top = "double depression"
  • SAD: episodes cluster in winter (or hypomania in summer, bipolar); first-line non-drug Tx is light therapy (morning, ~3 ft from face)
  • Peripartum onset: postpartum depression can occur up to a year after delivery (Townsend/ATI DSM specifier: pregnancy or within 4 wks); elevated suicide/rare infanticide risk — needs infant-safety assessment, not just routine follow-up

cards.prompt: What are the four symptom domains of depression, with one example finding in each?
cards.promptHtml: What are the four symptom domains of depression, with one example finding in each?
cards.answerHtml:
• Emotional: sad/hopeless mood, anhedonia, irritability
  • Cognitive: guilt/rumination, hopelessness, impaired concentration (can mimic dementia in older adults — "pseudodementia")
  • Behavioral: social withdrawal, declining occupational function, psychomotor agitation or retardation
  • Physical: sleep disturbance (initial/middle/terminal insomnia), fatigue, appetite/weight change

cards.prompt: What are the main biologic and psychosocial theories of the etiology of depression?
cards.promptHtml: What are the main biologic and psychosocial theories of the etiology of depression?
cards.answerHtml:
• Genetic: heritable, no single gene
  • Neurobiologic: norepinephrine/dopamine/serotonin dysregulation; Neuroendocrine: HPA/HPT/HPG axis dysregulation; Psychoneuroimmunology: ↑inflammatory cytokines
  • Psychodynamic: early lack of love/care, anger turned inward; Behavioral: loss of reward restricts activity, a self-reinforcing cycle
  • Cognitive (basis of CBT): irrational, negatively distorted beliefs; Object loss: abandonment in first 6 months of life

cards.prompt: What are the key nursing communication and nutrition strategies for depression and acute mania?
cards.promptHtml: What are the key nursing communication and nutrition strategies for depression and acute mania?
cards.answerHtml:
• Communication: be genuinely present, sit with silence; avoid false reassurance ("Everything will be fine!" is wrong); offer simple structured choices, not open-ended questions; make observations rather than direct questions; schedule activities for the afternoon (energy lowest early in day)
  • Nutrition — depression: appetite/weight change >5% body weight/month; monitor intake objectively, not by self-report
  • Nutrition — mania: can't sit still to eat; offer high-calorie, high-protein finger foods/drinks eaten while moving; weigh daily

cards.prompt: How do bipolar I, bipolar II, cyclothymic disorder, mania, and hypomania differ?
cards.promptHtml: How do bipolar I, bipolar II, cyclothymic disorder, mania, and hypomania differ?
cards.answerHtml:
• Bipolar I: ≥1 manic episode; depressive episode common but not required
  • Bipolar II: predominantly depressive course + brief hypomanic (not full manic) periods; often misdiagnosed as unipolar depression
  • Cyclothymic disorder: ≥2 years of hypomanic/depressive periods, none severe enough for full bipolar or MDD criteria
  • Mania vs hypomania: mania lasts ≥1 week (any length if hospitalized), marked impairment, often psychotic; hypomania is milder/briefer with no marked impairment and intact judgment

cards.prompt: How many Criterion B symptoms are required to diagnose a manic episode, and what mnemonic lists them?
cards.promptHtml: How many Criterion B symptoms are required to diagnose a manic episode, and what mnemonic lists them?
cards.answerHtml:
• ≥3 of 7 symptoms (≥4 if mood is only irritable, not elevated)
  • DIGFAST: Distractibility, Impulsivity/Indiscretion, Grandiosity, Flight of ideas, Activity increase, Sleep deficit, Talkativeness (pressured speech)
  • A mixed episode is mania + depression together — produces high suicide risk

cards.prompt: What is a "mood disorder due to another medical condition," and what should new-onset mania in an older adult after a stroke make the nurse suspect?
cards.promptHtml: What is a "mood disorder due to another medical condition," and what should new-onset mania in an older adult after a stroke make the nurse suspect?
cards.answerHtml:
• Mania or depression caused directly by a medical illness (thyroid dysfunction, CNS tumor, stroke) or a substance, rather than arising independently
  • New mania after a stroke/brain lesion suggests secondary mania, not primary bipolar disorder
  • Right-sided limbic, basal ganglia, or thalamic lesions are implicated

cards.prompt: What are the main biologic and psychosocial theories of the etiology of bipolar disorder?
cards.promptHtml: What are the main biologic and psychosocial theories of the etiology of bipolar disorder?
cards.answerHtml:
• Genetic: twin concordance 40–70% (Boyd) vs 60–90% (Townsend) — highly heritable either way
  • Chronobiologic: circadian disruption/sleep deprivation precipitates mania; seasonal light change can trigger winter depression or summer hypomania
  • Kindling: repeated episodes lower the threshold for the next, so later episodes need less or no stressor
  • BAS dysregulation: overreactive reward system drives mania, its deactivation drives depression
  • Social rhythm disruption: disrupting daily cues (wake time, meals, contact) destabilizes the circadian clock and triggers episodes

cards.prompt: What are the nursing priorities for an acutely manic patient (safety, environment, physical needs, and comorbidity)?
cards.promptHtml: What are the nursing priorities for an acutely manic patient (safety, environment, physical needs, and comorbidity)?
cards.answerHtml:
• Priority: protection of the patient and others is always first; approach calmly with firm, clear, simple limits; redirect rather than argue grandiose/tangential statements; reduce stimulation (lighting, noise, people)
  • Physical needs: monitor hydration, weigh daily; quiet low-stimulation environment with structured rest, no caffeine; remove hazardous objects (belts, shoestrings, smoking materials) and protect against poor judgment (giving away money, sexual indiscretion)
  • Comorbidity: alcohol/marijuana use and anxiety are common, worsen course, and complicate adherence/remission

cards.prompt: What are the suicide risk factors for depression, and which patient populations carry the highest or most easily missed risk?
cards.promptHtml: What are the suicide risk factors for depression, and which patient populations carry the highest or most easily missed risk?
cards.answerHtml:
• Risk factors: family/personal history of attempts; comorbid anxiety/panic, substance use, or psychosis; poor self-esteem, lack of social support, chronic medical illness
  • Geriatric clients: highest suicide risk of any group; symptoms easily confused with dementia/stroke
  • Youth: present with anxiety/somatic complaints and irritability more than sadness
  • PTSD/trauma-impacted and LGBTQ+ clients: elevated risk tied to environment and lack of support

cards.prompt: What is the correct nursing approach to assessing suicidal thoughts, and why?
cards.promptHtml: What is the correct nursing approach to assessing suicidal thoughts, and why?
cards.answerHtml:
• Ask directly and nonjudgmentally: "Have you thought about killing yourself? What is your plan? Do you have the means? How strong is your intent to die?"
  • Direct questions do NOT plant the idea — they are the only reliable way to surface risk hidden behind somatic complaints
  • Risk rises with a developed plan, strong intent, and available means

cards.prompt: When is suicide risk greatest for a patient with MDD — and why do two sources disagree?
cards.promptHtml: When is suicide risk greatest for a patient with MDD — and why do two sources disagree?
cards.answerHtml:
• Boyd: risk can rise as energy returns during recovery, because the patient now has the energy to act on suicidal thoughts; a sudden calm after intense distress is a warning sign (lecture)
  • (ATI: risk is greatest during the acute phase, when symptoms are most severe)
  • Know both framings; ATI-style practice items key "acute phase"

cards.prompt: What inpatient safety measures protect a client with active suicidal ideation, and why is postpartum psychosis a distinct emergency?
cards.promptHtml: What inpatient safety measures protect a client with active suicidal ideation, and why is postpartum psychosis a distinct emergency?
cards.answerHtml:
• Inpatient safety: room assignment close to the nurses' station, not private; 15-minute checks at irregular intervals (not predictable), especially nights, shift change, busy periods; remove sharps/belts/ties/glass; supervise meals and medication closely (confirm swallowing)
  • Postpartum psychosis: rare (1–2 per 1,000 deliveries) but 30–50% recurrence risk at the next delivery; infanticide/suicide risk is high enough to require urgent psychiatric evaluation and infant-safety planning

cards.prompt: What are the indications for ECT, and how does rTMS offer a less invasive alternative?
cards.promptHtml: What are the indications for ECT, and how does rTMS offer a less invasive alternative?
cards.answerHtml:
• ECT indications: severe, refractory, or psychotic/catatonic depression; mania/depression needing a rapid response (malnutrition, catatonia, active suicidality); bipolar rapid cycling (≥4 episodes/yr) or mania unresponsive to meds; NOT first-line — reserved for failed drug trials or unstable patients
  • rTMS: magnetic field induces cortical current to treat depression when medication/psychotherapy fail; patient stays awake — no anesthesia or seizure induction; given daily, outpatient

cards.prompt: What happens before and during ECT (consent, prep, medications, and airway management)?
cards.promptHtml: What happens before and during ECT (consent, prep, medications, and airway management)?
cards.answerHtml:
• Before: informed consent (next-of-kin/court order if involuntary); NPO after midnight (Townsend: 6–8h); pre-ECT workup (labs, ECG, chest x-ray); dentures removed; atropine/glycopyrrolate ~30 min prior (↓secretions, blunts vagal bradycardia); short-acting anesthetic, e.g. methohexital (ATI: etomidate/propofol)
  • During: short-acting muscle relaxant (succinylcholine) prevents injury from muscle contractions — NOT for sedation; it also paralyzes respiratory muscles, so the nurse assists ventilation with 100% O2 until spontaneous respirations return; EEG/ECG monitor seizure and cardiac activity

cards.prompt: What are the expected findings after ECT, and is permanent memory loss a settled issue?
cards.promptHtml: What are the expected findings after ECT, and is permanent memory loss a settled issue?
cards.answerHtml:
• Expected: headache, nausea, muscle soreness, transient confusion, brief hypertension, and retrograde amnesia around the treatment; alert ~15 min after
  • Boyd: memory loss is the most troublesome long-term effect; many have none, some report loss for months or years, and the evidence conflicts (ATI: permanent loss is "controversial"; most recover)
  • ECT is not a cure — maintenance ECT sustains the effect

cards.prompt: In the Consuela case (severe mania, ECT recommended but refused), what right does a psychiatric patient retain over treatment decisions?
cards.promptHtml: In the Consuela case (severe mania, ECT recommended but refused), what right does a psychiatric patient retain over treatment decisions?
cards.answerHtml:
• A psychiatric diagnosis alone does NOT strip decision-making rights
  • Unless a court has specifically found the patient incompetent for this decision, she retains the right to refuse ECT, even while hospitalized for her own safety
  • Override only via the legal process for involuntary treatment, not clinical consensus; overriding a competent refusal risks destroying trust and the therapeutic relationship

cards.prompt: How is grief differentiated from major depression, and what is pathological grief?
cards.promptHtml: How is grief differentiated from major depression, and what is pathological grief?
cards.answerHtml:
• Normal/uncomplicated grief: can mimic depression (sadness, rumination, insomnia, poor appetite); DSM-5 allows this — clinician judgment + cultural norms before diagnosing MDD on a loss; resolves ~12 wks, self-esteem intact, guilt specific to the loss
  • Complicated grief: often >3–6 months; idealization, denial, excessive guilt/anger, impaired function; risk factors: unresolved anger, poor support, ambivalence toward the deceased
  • Bereavement overload: unresolved grief from multiple losses stacking before any one resolves
  • Kübler-Ross stages: Denial/isolation → Anger → Bargaining → Depression (a passing stage, not automatic pathology) → Acceptance

cards.prompt: Where are mood disorders mainly managed, and what trend is reshaping that care?
cards.promptHtml: Where are mood disorders mainly managed, and what trend is reshaping that care?
cards.answerHtml:
• Case management: most depressive disorders are first identified and treated in primary care, not psychiatric settings — collaborative, interdisciplinary care is emphasized; bipolar relapse prevention relies on psychoeducation and stable social rhythms (sleep, meals, routine)
  • Trend: integrated primary/behavioral health care — co-locating or coordinating psychiatric care in primary care improves access and follow-through

cards.prompt: What are the diagnostic criteria for panic disorder, and what accompanies a panic attack physically?
cards.promptHtml: What are the diagnostic criteria for panic disorder, and what accompanies a panic attack physically?
cards.answerHtml:
• Recurrent, unexpected panic attacks: abrupt fear peaking within minutes (usually ~10, up to 30 min); first attack usually has an identifiable cue (asthma episode, first drug use)
  • Followed by ≥1 month of persistent worry about more attacks, or a maladaptive behavior change
  • ≥4 of 13 symptoms: palpitations, sweating, trembling, dyspnea, chest pain, nausea, dizziness, paresthesias, derealization, fear of dying/"going crazy"
  • Hyperventilation → compensated respiratory alkalosis (low CO2/bicarb, near-normal pH); mimics a heart attack, cardiac workup negative

cards.prompt: How do specific phobia, social anxiety disorder, and agoraphobia differ?
cards.promptHtml: How do specific phobia, social anxiety disorder, and agoraphobia differ?
cards.answerHtml:
• Specific phobia: fear of one circumscribed object/situation (animal, blood-injection-injury, etc.)
  • Social anxiety disorder: fear of scrutiny/embarrassment in social or performance situations
  • Agoraphobia: fear in ≥2 situations where escape would be hard (public transport, crowds, lines, open/enclosed spaces) → avoidance, potentially housebound

cards.prompt: What are the diagnostic criteria for generalized anxiety disorder (GAD)?
cards.promptHtml: What are the diagnostic criteria for generalized anxiety disorder (GAD)?
cards.answerHtml:
• Excessive worry and apprehension about multiple real-life matters for at least 6 months
  • Somatic symptoms: muscle aches, GI complaints, poor sleep, irritability, trembling, poor concentration, exaggerated startle
  • Often first seen in primary care, described as a "chronic worrier"

cards.prompt: What biologic and psychosocial factors predispose a person to panic disorder, and what are primary and secondary gain?
cards.promptHtml: What biologic and psychosocial factors predispose a person to panic disorder, and what are primary and secondary gain?
cards.answerHtml:
• Biologic: ~48% heritability; fear-network abnormalities (amygdala, hippocampus, thalamus); serotonin, norepinephrine, GABA involvement; HPA axis activation
  • Psychosocial: classical conditioning, interoceptive conditioning (body sensations become cues), catastrophic misinterpretation of mild sensations; triggers: caffeine, stimulants, decongestants, withdrawal from CNS depressants
  • Primary gain: the person's own motivation to relieve anxiety; secondary gain: attention/support received BECAUSE of illness — can paradoxically decrease motivation to recover if a nurse rewards helplessness

cards.prompt: What is the universal first nursing outcome for anxiety disorders, and what happens physically during a blood-injection-injury phobia reaction?
cards.promptHtml: What is the universal first nursing outcome for anxiety disorders, and what happens physically during a blood-injection-injury phobia reaction?
cards.answerHtml:
• Safety (free of self-harm) is the universal first outcome across panic, OCD, and PTSD care plans; recovery means functioning despite symptoms, not eliminating every trigger — for a specific phobia, avoiding the stimulus with minimal lifestyle disruption is a valid long-term goal if full exposure isn't the client's choice
  • Blood-injection-injury phobia: a vasovagal response (BP/pulse rise, then drop); ~75% faint — have the client lie down and monitor closely during the procedure

cards.prompt: How do obsessions and compulsions differ, and what is the diagnostic threshold and predisposing factors for OCD?
cards.promptHtml: How do obsessions and compulsions differ, and what is the diagnostic threshold and predisposing factors for OCD?
cards.answerHtml:
• Obsessions: excessive, unwanted, intrusive, persistent thoughts/impulses/images causing anxiety, not under the person's control
  • Compulsions: repetitive behaviors/mental acts performed ritualistically to prevent or relieve that anxiety
  • Diagnostic threshold: obsessions/compulsions take >1 hour/day or cause significant distress
  • Predisposing: familial link to Tourette syndrome; response to serotonergic drugs in 40–60% supports a serotonin link; a subset of children develop pediatric acute-onset neuropsychiatric syndrome after streptococcal or other infections

cards.prompt: What is the correct nursing approach to a newly admitted OCD patient's rituals, and what is "family accommodation"?
cards.promptHtml: What is the correct nursing approach to a newly admitted OCD patient's rituals, and what is "family accommodation"?
cards.answerHtml:
• At least initially, do NOT prevent the ritual — blocking it escalates anxiety; empathize with the need for it, schedule time for it, then collaborate on gradually limiting it (case: locking the bathroom to stop showers caused panic, discharge AMA)
  • Family accommodation: family adjusting routines around the client's rituals (e.g., re-checking locks for them); worsens outcomes by reinforcing rituals — teach families to reduce it while supporting treatment

cards.prompt: What are the four symptom clusters required to diagnose PTSD?
cards.promptHtml: What are the four symptom clusters required to diagnose PTSD?
cards.answerHtml:
• Intrusion: flashbacks, nightmares, dissociative reactions, distress at cues
  • Avoidance and numbing
  • Negative mood/cognition: guilt, shame, inability to feel positive emotions, "no one can be trusted"
  • Hyperarousal/hypervigilance: startle, irritability, aggression, sleep disturbance
  • Must follow exposure to actual/threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence

cards.prompt: How long must symptoms last to diagnose PTSD versus acute stress disorder (ASD)?
cards.promptHtml: How long must symptoms last to diagnose PTSD versus acute stress disorder (ASD)?
cards.answerHtml:
• ASD: anxiety, detachment, and related manifestations for at least 3 days but not more than 1 month after the trauma
  • PTSD: the same clinical picture lasting longer than 1 month — can persist for years
  • ASD can progress to PTSD if symptoms do not resolve within that window

cards.prompt: What predisposes a person to PTSD, what protects against it, and what does trauma-informed care mean in practice?
cards.promptHtml: What predisposes a person to PTSD, what protects against it, and what does trauma-informed care mean in practice?
cards.answerHtml:
• Risk: prior acute stress disorder; extent/duration/intensity of trauma; female sex (~2x); childhood abuse/ACEs; sleep disturbance pre-trauma; ~33% develop PTSD after sexual relationship violence vs ~3% for civilians after organized violence
  • Protective: resilience (positive self-concept, sense of control, social support)
  • Trauma-informed care: assume a trauma history, ask "what happened to you" not "what is wrong with you"; avoid retraumatization (restraint/locked units can retraumatize); let the survivor control disclosure pacing — meaning matters more than facts

cards.prompt: What distinguishes BDD, hoarding, trichotillomania, and excoriation as OCD-related disorders?
cards.promptHtml: What distinguishes BDD, hoarding, trichotillomania, and excoriation as OCD-related disorders?
cards.answerHtml:
• Body dysmorphic disorder: preoccupation with a slight/imagined flaw; surgery does not help; high suicide risk
  • Hoarding: a fire/safety hazard; home health nurses often detect it first; more common in males (an exception to the usual female predominance)
  • Trichotillomania: hair pulling with relief; hairballs can cause GI obstruction
  • Excoriation: repetitive skin picking

cards.prompt: What breathing, lifestyle, cognitive, and grounding techniques are taught for anxiety management?
cards.promptHtml: What breathing, lifestyle, cognitive, and grounding techniques are taught for anxiety management?
cards.answerHtml:
• Breathing: abdominal breathing (slow nasal inhale, abdomen rises, pause, exhale pursed lips, 10 breaths) and four-square breathing (inhale/hold/exhale/rest 4 each)
  • Lifestyle: exercise 10–20 min 2–3x/wk (↓tension, ↑serotonin/endorphins); regular balanced meals (avoid hypoglycemia), taper caffeine; sleep hygiene (regular schedule, no alcohol/late caffeine/nicotine)
  • Cognitive: distraction, reframing away from "should" statements, positive self-talk cards
  • 5-4-3-2-1 grounding: for acute panic — name 5 seen/4 touched/3 heard/2 smelled/1 tasted; pair with reassurance, staying present, reduced stimulation, no touch

cards.prompt: What is the correct nursing intervention sequence for a patient having a panic attack?
cards.promptHtml: What is the correct nursing intervention sequence for a patient having a panic attack?
cards.answerHtml:
• Stay with the patient; remain calm yourself
  • Reassure using short, simple directions
  • Walk the patient to a quiet, low-stimulation area
  • Do not say "you're fine" or try to argue the fear away — acknowledge the symptoms are real and frightening

cards.prompt: Why is suicide screening a universal priority across panic disorder, OCD, and PTSD, and what is the evidence-based approach to treating panic attacks?
cards.promptHtml: Why is suicide screening a universal priority across panic disorder, OCD, and PTSD, and what is the evidence-based approach to treating panic attacks?
cards.answerHtml:
• Suicide screening: first priority in panic disorder and PTSD care, must also be assessed in OCD; ~1 in 5 clients experiencing panic report suicidality; alcohol/substance use combined with PTSD further raises risk
  • Treatment: CBT + medication is first-line; telehealth delivers most of this effectively and is especially useful since face-to-face care itself raises anxiety for some patients; NAMI and ADAA are credible patient resources, group psychotherapy also effective

cards.prompt: Where is most anxiety-disorder care delivered, and what should the nurse know about anxiety in geriatric patients?
cards.promptHtml: Where is most anxiety-disorder care delivered, and what should the nurse know about anxiety in geriatric patients?
cards.answerHtml:
• Care setting: most people with panic disorder and PTSD are treated in the community and primary care, the least restrictive setting; nurses run psychoeducation groups, advanced practice nurses deliver CBT; home-based exposure therapy works as well as clinic-based exposure therapy
  • Geriatric: anxiety prevalence declines with age but still co-occurs heavily with depression and pain, raising suicide risk; comorbid dementia compounds impairment; late-onset OCD (after age 50) warrants a workup for underlying brain pathology

cards.prompt: Delirium vs. dementia: underlying cause and course
cards.promptHtml: Delirium vs. dementia: underlying cause and course
cards.answerHtml:
Dementia and delirium are differentiated by underlying cause, not symptom pattern.

  • Delirium: acute disturbance from a medical cause/substance; sudden onset (hours-days); fluctuating course over 24h; usually reversible
  • Dementia: chronic decline from a specific etiology (e.g., Alzheimer disease); insidious onset; stable course over 24h; generally irreversible

cards.prompt: Delirium vs. dementia: consciousness, attention, and nursing priority
cards.promptHtml: Delirium vs. dementia: consciousness, attention, and nursing priority
cards.answerHtml:
• Delirium: reduced consciousness; inattentive (can't focus/sustain/shift attention); usually reversible if cause found/treated
  • Dementia: clear consciousness; attention normal until late disease; progressive, irreversible

Nursing priority: sudden confusion with fluctuating drowsiness/agitation (e.g., post-op) -- get vitals, O2 sat, glucose, notify provider. Delirium is a medical emergency; don't assume dementia or restrain.

cards.prompt: Depression vs. dementia (pseudodementia)
cards.promptHtml: Depression vs. dementia (pseudodementia)
cards.answerHtml:
Memory complaints in older adults are more often from depression than from normal aging, and are commonly mistaken for "old age." Depression mimicking dementia is called "pseudodementia" (lecture, Boyd, Townsend).

  • Depression: complains of memory loss and has more insight into the deficits (Boyd, Townsend); emphasizes deficits, "I don't know" answers, poor effort despite being capable (verify)
  • Dementia: often unaware of deficits, may confabulate to cover memory gaps
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Superimposed delirium on existing dementia
cards.promptHtml: Superimposed delirium on existing dementia
cards.answerHtml: A patient with known Alzheimer disease who suddenly becomes more confused/agitated should be suspected of superimposed delirium (e.g., dehydration, infection, pain, new medication reaction) -- not simple disease progression. Preexisting dementia is one of the greatest risk factors for delirium.

cards.prompt: DSM-5-TR neurocognitive spectrum terminology
cards.promptHtml: DSM-5-TR neurocognitive spectrum terminology
cards.answerHtml: DSM-5-TR uses three diagnoses across the neurocognitive spectrum: delirium, mild neurocognitive disorder (mild cognitive impairment), and major neurocognitive disorder (dementia), given with an etiologic specifier, e.g., "due to Alzheimer disease". The separate DSM-IV "amnestic disorder" category was folded into major/mild NCD (verify).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Delirium subtypes
cards.promptHtml: Delirium subtypes
cards.answerHtml:
• Hyperactive: agitated, heightened arousal
  • Hypoactive: somnolent, psychomotor slow (most common AND most often missed)
  • Mixed: alternates between the two
  • Unclassified (ATI): doesn't fit the other three

cards.prompt: Dementia (major NCD): diagnostic criteria
cards.promptHtml: Dementia (major NCD): diagnostic criteria
cards.answerHtml:
Criteria (syllabus, DSM-IV style): memory impairment (required) PLUS 1+ of: aphasia, apraxia, agnosia, or disturbed executive function.

Progression: losing valuables -> forgetting an activity in progress (stove, water running) -> lost in familiar places -> severe: forgetting occupation, birthday, family, own name.

Rule out before diagnosing: physical illness, vitamin deficiency, substance, major depression, or schizophrenia. Imaging typically shows brain atrophy, enlarged ventricles.

cards.prompt: Vascular neurocognitive disorder vs. Alzheimer disease
cards.promptHtml: Vascular neurocognitive disorder vs. Alzheimer disease
cards.answerHtml:
• Vascular: sudden, step-like decline from a series of small strokes/TIAs; intermittent/fluctuating; manage vascular risk factors (BP, glucose, stroke prevention)
  • Alzheimer: insidious onset, steady gradual decline

cards.prompt: Lewy body and frontotemporal neurocognitive disorder vs. Alzheimer disease
cards.promptHtml: Lewy body and frontotemporal neurocognitive disorder vs. Alzheimer disease
cards.answerHtml:
• Lewy body: visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, spontaneous parkinsonism, fluctuating attention (resembles delirium), falls/syncope, orthostatic hypotension; marked, dangerous sensitivity to antipsychotic medication
  • Frontotemporal: early personality/behavior change, apathy or disinhibition, socially inappropriate behavior with little insight, planning/judgment deficits -- memory relatively preserved early (unlike AD, where memory loss comes first)

cards.prompt: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome
cards.promptHtml: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome
cards.answerHtml:
Alcohol-related amnestic disorder from thiamine deficiency.

  • Wernicke (acute): vision changes, ataxia, hypotension, confusion; can progress to coma; often reversible if treated early
  • Korsakoff (chronic): amnesia, inability to learn new information, confabulation (e.g., a heavy-alcohol-use patient fluently describing a fishing trip that never happened)

cards.prompt: Nursing attitude and safety blind spots with cognitively impaired patients
cards.promptHtml: Nursing attitude and safety blind spots with cognitively impaired patients
cards.answerHtml:
• Ageism/elderspeak ("confusion is just old age," baby talk) damages communication and can mask treatable delirium or depression
  • Disruptive behavior (vocalizing, resisting care) is communication of an unmet need (pain, fatigue, hunger), not just "difficult" behavior
  • Passive suicide (self-starvation, nonadherence) is prevalent in older adults, including those with cognitive/mood changes, and easy to miss because it doesn't look like an overt attempt

cards.prompt: Cognitive/delirium screening tools: SPMSQ, MMSE, CAM
cards.promptHtml: Cognitive/delirium screening tools: SPMSQ, MMSE, CAM
cards.answerHtml:
• SPMSQ: 10 questions (orientation, personal facts, president); 0-2 errors normal, 3-4 mild, 5-7 moderate, 8+ severe (allow 1 extra error if <=grade school education; 1 fewer if beyond high school)
  • MMSE (dementia/cognition): 24-30 normal; 18-23 mild impairment (Psych Notes: mild/moderate); 0-17 severe
  • CAM (delirium): acute onset/fluctuating course + inattention, plus disorganized thinking OR altered consciousness (verify)
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Communication strategies for delirium and dementia
cards.promptHtml: Communication strategies for delirium and dementia
cards.answerHtml:
• Do not argue a false belief (e.g., "My mother is waiting for me"); validate the underlying feeling and redirect (ask about happy memories) -- arguing escalates distress/agitation
  • Short, simple sentences, one piece of information at a time; limit choices
  • Delirium: introduce yourself at every contact; approach slowly from the front, say the patient's name before touching
  • Calm, reassuring tone; never argue with hallucinations/delusions

cards.prompt: Dementia wandering: safety strategies
cards.promptHtml: Dementia wandering: safety strategies
cards.answerHtml:
• Supervision and electronically controlled/alarmed exits; label doors and rooms
  • Verbal/visual redirection rather than restraint or sedation
  • Home: install door locks up high (out of reach), remove scatter rugs, secure cords, lock away cleaning supplies
  • Wandering is often goal-seeking (looking for a bathroom or room)

cards.prompt: Caregiver support and nursing home placement triggers
cards.promptHtml: Caregiver support and nursing home placement triggers
cards.answerHtml: Family caregivers of patients with dementia are sometimes called "copatients": they have poorer quality of life than age-matched peers and carry caregiver role strain (a NANDA diagnosis), with risk for burnout, isolation, and elder abuse. Support with education, respite care, day care, support groups. Placement is often triggered by unmanageable incontinence and behaviors such as wandering and aggression; 60-70% of people with Alzheimer disease live at home, ~86% of that care from family/friends.

cards.prompt: Alzheimer disease: case management
cards.promptHtml: Alzheimer disease: case management
cards.answerHtml:
Goal: continuity of care: access to services across an unpredictable, changing course

Nurse's role:

  • advocate on care, safety, and reimbursement issues
  • often involved with the Alzheimer's Association

Primary care vs. specialist:

  • primary care treats dementia until behavioral disturbances emerge, then refers to mental health/geriatric specialists for the psychiatric symptoms
  • primary care keeps the medical care; if meds are used, the primary care nurse monitors target symptoms, side effects, and drug-drug interactions

cards.prompt: Cognitive disorders: non-drug care trends
cards.promptHtml: Cognitive disorders: non-drug care trends
cards.answerHtml:
• Cognitive reserve: protect it with exercise, education, and cognitive stimulation
  • Complementary therapies: aromatherapy, massage, acupuncture, therapeutic touch reduce agitation/aggression in delirium
  • Person-centered care: e.g., adapting bathing (a high-risk time for agitation in late AD) to the resident's preferences
  • Research: gut-brain axis and nutrition

cards.prompt: Dissociative amnesia (incl. dissociative fugue)
cards.promptHtml: Dissociative amnesia (incl. dissociative fugue)
cards.answerHtml:
Inability to recall important, usually stressful, personal information -- too extensive for ordinary forgetting; linked to trauma (e.g., childhood sexual abuse).

  • Localized/Selective: gaps tied to, or details within, one period of trauma
  • Generalized (rare): erases identity and life memories
  • Continuous: forgetting each new event as it happens
  • Systematized: losing memories tied to one category/person

DSM-5 treats fugue (sudden unexplained travel from home, identity confusion, or new identity) as a specifier of dissociative amnesia; the syllabus and lecture list "Dissociative Fugue" as its own diagnosis.

cards.prompt: Dissociative identity disorder (DID): criteria and safety
cards.promptHtml: Dissociative identity disorder (DID): criteria and safety
cards.answerHtml:
Criteria: 2+ distinct identity states, each with its own way of relating to the environment, plus inability to recall important personal information too extensive for ordinary forgetting.

Safety: 85%-97% of adults with DID have a documented history of physical and/or sexual abuse -- priority is assessing for suicidal ideation and self-injury, both risks in dissociative disorders.

cards.prompt: DID treatment goal
cards.promptHtml: DID treatment goal
cards.answerHtml: Goal is integration -- bringing all identity states together into one. Typically pursued through hypnosis, plus CBT or psychodynamic psychotherapy to identify triggers of anxiety and dissociation. Build trust with the original personality and each alter: each sees itself as a separate entity and is initially treated as such; reassure alters they will be integrated, not destroyed. Do not force recall of trauma memories.

cards.prompt: Dissociative safety priorities: recovered memory and self-injury
cards.promptHtml: Dissociative safety priorities: recovered memory and self-injury
cards.answerHtml:
• Sudden recovery of a repressed traumatic memory -> patient becomes tearful/withdrawn: assess for suicidal ideation FIRST (sudden recovery can overwhelm and trigger suicidal thoughts); address safety before exploring the memory
  • Patient uses self-injury to "refocus" while dissociating: priority is safety (risk for self-mutilation) -- observe for self-harm, remove dangerous objects, build safer-choice strategies, and teach grounding substitutes: 5-4-3-2-1, deep breathing (lecture); clapping or touching objects (ATI)

cards.prompt: Depersonalization/derealization disorder
cards.promptHtml: Depersonalization/derealization disorder
cards.answerHtml: Persistent/recurrent feelings of detachment from one's own mental processes (depersonalization) or that surroundings are unreal (derealization). Reality testing stays intact -- the patient knows the feeling isn't literally true (verify).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Somatic symptom disorder (incl. pain disorder)
cards.promptHtml: Somatic symptom disorder (incl. pain disorder)
cards.answerHtml:
Syllabus "Somatoform Disorder" = DSM-IV somatization disorder; DSM-5: somatic symptom disorder (group: "somatic symptom and related disorders"). Syllabus criteria: onset before age 30, pain at 4+ sites, 2+ GI symptoms, 1+ sexual/reproductive symptom, 1+ pseudoneurologic symptom; symptoms not intentionally produced. DSM-5: no symptom count; excessive thoughts/feelings/behaviors 6+ mo. "Pain Disorder" is no longer stand-alone -- folded in with a predominant pain specifier; pain is the single most common finding and rarely responds to analgesics long-term.

Manage: centralize care with one primary provider/regular visits (not symptom-driven), retrieve records; mental health consults validate the diagnosis to avoid unnecessary testing.

cards.prompt: Illness anxiety disorder (formerly hypochondriasis)
cards.promptHtml: Illness anxiety disorder (formerly hypochondriasis)
cards.answerHtml:
Preoccupation with having/developing a serious illness, 6+ months, despite medical reassurance, with deterioration of the doctor-patient relationship. Syllabus term "Hypochondriasis" is now Illness Anxiety Disorder (minimal somatic symptoms) or Somatic Symptom Disorder (if somatic symptoms are prominent).

  • Health-seeking type: frequent medical visits and diagnostic testing
  • Care-avoidant type: avoids all provider contact because the contact itself raises anxiety

cards.prompt: Conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder)
cards.promptHtml: Conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder)
cards.answerHtml:
Neurologic symptoms (paralysis, aphonia, blindness, seizures) with negative workup and a non-anatomic pattern (e.g., a "paralyzed" limb keeps normal reflexes/tone); may show la belle indifference -- a lack of concern about the symptom's implications.

  • Good prognosis: paralysis, aphonia, or blindness; acute onset; identified stressor; immediate treatment; above-average intelligence
  • Poor prognosis: tremor or seizures

cards.prompt: Body dysmorphic disorder
cards.promptHtml: Body dysmorphic disorder
cards.answerHtml: Preoccupation with an imagined or slight defect in appearance (mirror checking, excessive grooming, comparing self to others, avoiding social activities). Historically grouped with somatoform disorders (syllabus, lecture); DSM-5 reclassifies it as an obsessive-compulsive related disorder.

cards.prompt: Somatic symptom and dissociative disorders: theories
cards.promptHtml: Somatic symptom and dissociative disorders: theories
cards.answerHtml:
Biologic:

  • cortico-limbic-cerebellar circuit deficits; familial risk (SSD)
  • trauma can impair the limbic system (dissociative)

Psychological:

  • somatization as emotional communication; learned sick-role behavior
  • alexithymia (can't identify/express emotions)
  • repression of feelings, conflicts, unacceptable impulses
  • chronic childhood trauma (dissociative)

Social/cultural: stigma of mental illness makes body symptoms more acceptable (e.g., neurasthenia in China, "nerves" in Latin America)

cards.prompt: What are reattribution treatment's four stages for somatic symptom disorder?
cards.promptHtml: What are reattribution treatment's four stages for somatic symptom disorder?
cards.answerHtml:
Goal: help the client link physical symptoms to psychological factors while feeling cared for and understood.

  • 1. Feeling understood: active listening, empathy, thorough symptom history focused on the client's view of the cause; brief physical check
  • 2. Broadening the agenda: acknowledge concerns; give feedback on findings
  • 3. Making the link: acknowledge the lack of a physical cause while preserving self-esteem
  • 4. Negotiating further treatment: plan with the provider and client, with regular follow-up visits

cards.prompt: Factitious disorder (incl. imposed on another)
cards.promptHtml: Factitious disorder (incl. imposed on another)
cards.answerHtml:
Individual intentionally feigns a physical/psychological illness to take on the sick role for personal (internal) gain, not an external reward. Core feature: pseudologia fantastica (fascinating, partly true/false stories of personal triumph).

Imposed on another (e.g., caregiver brings a child in for unwitnessed 'seizures' that resolve when caregiver is absent): ensure child safety and report suspected abuse -- a severe form of child abuse; child is often removed from the caregiver's care.

Nursing attitude: expect anger/betrayal toward these patients -- recognize it first so it doesn't undermine nonjudgmental care; avoid confrontation, build rapport, communicate with the whole team.

cards.prompt: Factitious disorder vs. malingering
cards.promptHtml: Factitious disorder vs. malingering
cards.answerHtml:
Malingering: intentional symptom production for a specific self-serving external goal (disability, avoiding work/duty) -- explicitly not a psychiatric disorder.

Distinguishing question is motive: external reward = malingering; internal need to occupy the sick role = factitious disorder.

cards.prompt: Primary gain vs. secondary gain
cards.promptHtml: Primary gain vs. secondary gain
cards.answerHtml:
Primary gain: internal relief — anxiety or an internal conflict is kept out of conscious awareness (lecture: symptoms keep psychological needs out of conscious awareness) (Townsend: excused from duties; ATI counts that as secondary gain).

Secondary gain: external benefits of being sick, e.g. support and attention from others (lecture), distraction from obligations (ATI).

Nursing approach: attend to the patient when NOT discussing symptoms and limit time spent on symptom talk, while recognizing the symptoms are real to the patient.

cards.prompt: Somatic symptom disorder: community-based care
cards.promptHtml: Somatic symptom disorder: community-based care
cards.answerHtml:
• Most patients are outpatients; hospital stays are usually for medical workups or comorbid disorders
  • Switching providers harms long-term care (see the SSD card: one primary provider)
  • Virtual care: relaxation, stress-reduction, sleep, and imagery apps reduce the intensity of distress; virtual primary care visits and health education add safe patient-clinician contact

cards.prompt: Somatic symptom and dissociative disorders: home care and family education
cards.promptHtml: Somatic symptom and dissociative disorders: home care and family education
cards.answerHtml:
SSD:

  • symptoms become the focus of family life (activities planned around the patient); family needs support and education about the disorder
  • teach strategies for the multiple complaints and better communication patterns
  • watch for current physical/sexual abuse (chaotic families)

Dissociative amnesia: get background from family/significant others (likes, important people, activities) to build a baseline; involve family in planning only with the patient's consent (verify)
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Somatic symptom and dissociative disorders: treatment trends
cards.promptHtml: Somatic symptom and dissociative disorders: treatment trends
cards.answerHtml:
• Primary care integration: a brief psychoeducation session in primary care reduced health anxiety, worry, loneliness, and pain
  • DID: now supported as a complex posttraumatic developmental disorder, with emerging evidence of structural brain changes
  • Conversion disorder (functional neurologic symptom disorder): some evidence of neurobiologic brain changes behind the symptoms

cards.prompt: Lithium carbonate (Lithobid; syllabus: Eskalith)
cards.promptHtml: Lithium carbonate (Lithobid; syllabus: Eskalith)
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Drug of choice for acute mania and maintenance therapy of bipolar disorder; also lowers suicide risk and has a mild antidepressant effect in bipolar depression.
  • Onset is slow (5–7 days, up to 2 weeks), so an antipsychotic or short-term benzodiazepine is often added until it takes effect.
  • Narrow therapeutic range; never stopped abruptly (see level and monitoring cards).

cards.prompt: What is lithium's therapeutic serum range during acute mania, and for maintenance therapy of bipolar disorder?
cards.promptHtml: What is lithium's therapeutic serum range during acute mania, and for maintenance therapy of bipolar disorder?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Therapeutic level: 0.6–1.2 mEq/L (lecture).
  • Acute mania may be run higher: about 0.8–1.4 mEq/L (Boyd Ch12). (Townsend/Psych Notes/ATI: 1.0–1.5.)
  • Levels above 1.5 mEq/L are treated as toxic.

cards.prompt: A patient started on lithium for acute mania has a serum level of 1.2 mEq/L. What should the nurse do?
cards.promptHtml: A patient started on lithium for acute mania has a serum level of 1.2 mEq/L. What should the nurse do?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Administer the next dose as scheduled.
  • 1.2 mEq/L is an expected level during acute mania — not a reason to withhold the dose or request a stat repeat level.

cards.prompt: What are the signs of mild lithium toxicity, roughly under 1.5 mEq/L?
cards.promptHtml: What are the signs of mild lithium toxicity, roughly under 1.5 mEq/L?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Metallic taste, fine hand tremor, nausea, polyuria/polydipsia, loose stools, muscle weakness, fatigue, weight gain, edema, memory problems.
  • These often overlap with expected early side effects and tend to improve over time.

cards.prompt: What are the signs of moderate lithium toxicity, roughly 1.5–2.5 mEq/L, and what should the nurse do?
cards.promptHtml: What are the signs of moderate lithium toxicity, roughly 1.5–2.5 mEq/L, and what should the nurse do?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Severe diarrhea/vomiting, drowsiness/sedation, muscle weakness, ataxia/poor coordination, coarse tremor, slurred speech, tinnitus, blurred vision, confusion, muscle twitching, asymmetric reflexes.
  • Withhold the dose, notify the provider, and obtain a repeat level.
  • ATI splits this band into early (1.5–2.0, withhold/notify) and advanced (2.0–2.5, acute care); Boyd treats 1.5–2.5 as one moderate band.

cards.prompt: What are the signs of severe, life-threatening lithium toxicity, above about 2.5 mEq/L, and how is it treated?
cards.promptHtml: What are the signs of severe, life-threatening lithium toxicity, above about 2.5 mEq/L, and how is it treated?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Cardiac arrhythmias, nystagmus, coarse tremor/fasciculations, visual or tactile hallucinations, oliguria progressing to renal failure, seizures, coma, death.
  • Hemodialysis is the definitive treatment; there is no antidote (verify).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: A patient on lithium has a level of 3.0 mEq/L. What does the nurse see, and what are the priority actions?
cards.promptHtml: A patient on lithium has a level of 3.0 mEq/L. What does the nurse see, and what are the priority actions?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Severe, life-threatening toxicity: above 2.5 mEq/L in both the ATI and Boyd bands.
  • Expect arrhythmias, nystagmus, coarse tremor/fasciculations, visual/tactile hallucinations, oliguria progressing to renal failure, seizures, rapid progression to coma and death.
  • Hold the next dose immediately; notify the provider; obtain a stat repeat level plus electrolytes/creatinine.
  • Assess airway/LOC, start seizure precautions (fall precautions and cardiac monitoring, verify), and push fluids (oral, or IV isotonic saline if the patient can't drink).
  • Severe toxicity is treated with hemodialysis.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: What definitive treatment is used for a lithium level of 3.0 mEq/L, and at what thresholds is it typically started?
cards.promptHtml: What definitive treatment is used for a lithium level of 3.0 mEq/L, and at what thresholds is it typically started?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Hemodialysis — the definitive treatment for severe lithium toxicity; there is no antidote (verify).
  • Boyd: may be necessary in severe toxicity; ATI: can be warranted above 2.5 mEq/L.
  • Common triggers: a level above 4.0 mEq/L, or above 2.5 mEq/L with seizures, dysrhythmias, decreased consciousness, or kidney impairment (verify).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: Why doesn't activated charcoal help treat a lithium level of 3.0 mEq/L?
cards.promptHtml: Why doesn't activated charcoal help treat a lithium level of 3.0 mEq/L?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Activated charcoal does not bind lithium (verify).
  • Management is supportive: IV fluids, possible gastric lavage after an acute ingestion, and hemodialysis for severe cases.
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: How long does it take for lithium toxicity to resolve once the drug is stopped, and what permanent damage can severe toxicity cause?
cards.promptHtml: How long does it take for lithium toxicity to resolve once the drug is stopped, and what permanent damage can severe toxicity cause?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Mild toxicity usually resolves within 24–48 hours of stopping lithium.
  • Severe toxicity can leave permanent neurologic (cerebellar) damage (verify).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: When should a trough lithium level be drawn relative to the last dose?
cards.promptHtml: When should a trough lithium level be drawn relative to the last dose?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • 10–12 hours after the last dose, in the morning, before the next (morning) dose.
  • In the hospital, the morning dose is held until the blood is drawn, to avoid a falsely high level.

cards.prompt: How often are lithium levels checked during initiation/acute treatment versus stable maintenance?
cards.promptHtml: How often are lithium levels checked during initiation/acute treatment versus stable maintenance?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.

  • Initiation/acute phase: twice weekly (Boyd Ch26, Townsend) until the therapeutic level is reached.
  • Stable maintenance: every 2 months (lecture). (Boyd Ch26: every 2–3 months.)
  • Recheck closely after any dose change (ATI), and after a new interacting drug or illness (verify).
cards.label: verify

cards.prompt: What baseline and ongoing lab work is needed for a patient starting lithium?
cards.promptHtml: What baseline and ongoing lab work is needed for a patient starting lithium?
cards.answerHtml:
Class: Mood stabilizer.
